claims.text: The as-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack under operational loads.
The as-cast alloy contains coarse grain boundaries with inhomogeneities.
Coarse grain-boundary inhomogeneities cause the alloy's poor load-bearing integrity and cracking.
The unchanged alloy has a large caloric response during applied-field and pressure-driven refrigeration cycles.
A tailored thermal or thermomechanical treatment can produce a minute nanoscale coherent secondary phase along the alloy's grain boundaries.

Treatment below a transformation-critical temperature, with controlled hold time and cooling rate, can promote precipitate nucleation and growth without changing the bulk transformation kinetics responsible for caloric performance.
The treatment will create a refined intergranular architecture consisting of nanoscale coherent precipitates distributed along grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary precipitates will act as crack-deflection and crack-pinning sites.
Crack deflection and pinning by the precipitates will strengthen the grain boundaries and improve toughness and crack resistance.
Carefully limiting thermal exposure will leave the grain interior largely unaltered.
Preserving the grain interior will preserve the reversible phase transformations responsible for the caloric response.
The treatment will improve fracture toughness by at least 20% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy's field-induced caloric response will differ by no more than 10% from that of the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy's pressure-induced caloric response will differ by no more than 10% from that of the untreated alloy.
The proposed benefits are applicable under magnetic or electric applied fields and pressure fields at refrigeration operating temperatures and operational mechanical loads.
Processing temperatures must remain below the threshold at which active phase-transformation kinetics are altered.
A controlled comparison of identically composed treated and untreated samples can test the proposed mechanical and caloric effects.
Failure to obtain at least a 20% mechanical-integrity improvement, or degradation of caloric response by more than 10%, would falsify the hypothesis.
